segments.text: Part 3. You will hear two geography students talking to their tutor about a survey they are doing on how students get to university. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

part.title: Planning a student travel survey

turns.text: Come in, Shannon, Mitchell. Have a seat. So, this is your survey on how students travel to campus. Remind me why you settled on that topic?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Well, we both drive in from out past Penrith, so we know the problem first-hand. But honestly, that wasn't the main reason.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No. The main thing was that the uni's deciding at the moment whether to build another multi-storey car park or spend the money on a shuttle bus, and we thought our results might actually feed into that.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's a good motivation. There's already plenty of research on student travel, so a link to a real decision helps. Now, you ran a pilot. How did that go?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Better than we expected in some ways. We were worried the wording would confuse people, but nobody asked us what anything meant.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: The real problem was the time. It took most people about twelve minutes, and a couple just gave up halfway through.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Twelve minutes is a lot to ask of someone between lectures. So you cut it down?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Yes, from twenty-two questions to fourteen. It's about five minutes now.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Good. And how have you been finding participants?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: We started by standing outside the library with a clipboard, but that was pretty slow. We only got fifteen or so in two afternoons.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: We also asked a few lecturers to mention it at the start of class, but they said they weren't allowed to. So in the end we put a link on the student union's online noticeboard, and that's where nearly all our responses have come from.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I see. And how many have you got so far?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: We set ourselves a target of 150. Last Friday we had about 60, and now we're up to 110.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's healthy. But I do have a concern about who's answering. Have you looked at the breakdown?
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: We checked faculties, and it's a fairly even spread. Science, arts, business, all roughly the same. And we left out anyone living in the residential colleges, since they don't really travel.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Sensible. But think about who reads the union noticeboard. It's mostly full-time students who are on campus every day. People studying part-time, often in the evenings, are hardly represented at all, and they're the group most likely to drive in after work.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.say: Right, that's true. We've only got about six part-timers. Could we offer a prize? Like a draw for a one hundred dollars voucher?
turns.text: Right, that's true. We've only got about six part-timers. Could we offer a prize? Like a draw for a $100 voucher?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: You could, but it would have to go back through the ethics committee, and that can take a month. You haven't got that long.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: What about handing out paper copies in the car park in the evening?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I wouldn't. People are tired and in a hurry, and you'd need permission from campus security. The simplest thing is to email the coordinators of the evening courses and ask them to forward the link to their students.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Okay, we'll do that this week.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right. Now, I've been through your fourteen questions, and I've got a few suggestions. The first one asks for their main way of getting here, and they tick one box. But lots of people catch a train and then cycle from the station, or drive to a park-and-ride.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: So we should add more options to the list?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, your list's fine as it is. The issue is that people need to be able to tick more than one.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Okay. Then there's the one on weekly travel costs.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.say: Yes. You ask for an exact dollar amount, and I suspect most people have no idea what they spend. Give them bands instead, say under twenty dollars, twenty dollars to forty dollars, and so on.
turns.text: Yes. You ask for an exact dollar amount, and I suspect most people have no idea what they spend. Give them bands instead, say under $20, $20 to $40, and so on.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: What about postcode? A few people in the pilot didn't like giving it, so we thought about dropping it altogether.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Don't drop it. It's the only way you'll be able to map where people come from. Just make it optional, so nobody feels pressured.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: And the question on why people chose their transport?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That one's really asking two different things: why they use their current method, and what would make them switch to something else. People only answer half of it. Make those two separate questions.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: Then there's satisfaction with the bus service. At the moment it's just an open box. Should we put in an example answer, so people know what to write?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: An example might lead them. I'd turn it into a rating scale, from one to five, so you can compare the answers easily.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: And the last one's distance from home to campus. We wondered about moving that to the start, since it's quick to answer.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Actually, you don't need it at all. If you've got the postcode, you can work out the distance yourselves, and people usually guess wrong anyway. So I'd take it out.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.text: So we lose one and gain one. That keeps us at fourteen, then.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Exactly. Send me the revised version by Friday, and we'll meet again next week.
turns.speaker: tutor

turns.heard: Come in, Shannon Mitchell, have a seat. So, this is your survey on how students travel to campus. Remind me why you settled on that topic?
Well, we both drive in from out past Penrith, so we know the problem firsthand. But honestly, that wasn't the main reason.

No, the main thing was that the uni's deciding at the moment whether to build another multi-storey car park or spend the money on a shuttle bus, and we thought our results might actually feed into that.
That's a good motivation. There's already plenty of research on student travel, so a link to a real decision helps. Now, you ran a pilot – how did that go?
Better than we expected in some ways. We were worried the wording would confuse people, but nobody asked us what anything meant!
The real problem was the time. It took most people about 12 minutes, and a couple just gave up halfway through.
Twelve minutes is a lot to ask of someone between lectures, so you cut it down?
Yes, from twenty-two questions to fourteen. It's about five minutes now.
Good. And how have you been finding participants?
We started by standing outside the library with a clipboard, but that was pretty slow. We only got fifteen or so in two afternoons.

We also asked a few lecturers to mention it at the start of class, but they said they weren't allowed to. So in the end, we put a link on the student union's online notice board, and that's where nearly all our responses have come from.
I see. And how many have you got so far?
We set ourselves a target of 150. Last Friday we had about 60, and now we're up to 110.
That's healthy, but I do have a concern about who's answering. Have you looked at the breakdown?
We checked faculties, and it's a fairly even spread - science, arts, business, all roughly the same. And we left out anyone living in the residential colleges, since they don't really travel.

Sensible, but think about who reads the union notice board. It's mostly full-time students who are on campus every day. People studying part-time, often in the evenings, are hardly represented at all, and they're the group most likely to drive in after work.
Right, that's true. We've only got about six part-timers. Could we offer a prize? Like a draw for a $100 voucher?
You could, but it would have to go back through the ethics committee, and that can take a month. You haven't got that long.
What about handing out paper copies in the car park in the evening?

I wouldn't. People are tired and in a hurry, and you'd need permission from campus security. The simplest thing is to email the coordinators of the evening courses and ask them to forward the link to their students.
Okay, we'll do that this week.

Right, now I've been through your fourteen questions and I've got a few suggestions. The first one asks for their main way of getting here, and they tick one box. But lots of people catch a train and then cycle from the station, or drive to a park and ride.
So we should add more options to the list?
No, your list's fine as it is. The issue is that people need to be able to tick more than one.
Okay, then there's the one on weekly travel costs.
Yes, you ask for an exact dollar amount, and I suspect most people have no idea what they spend. Give them bands instead, say, under $20, $20 to $40, and so on
What about postcode? A few people in the pilot didn’t like giving it, so we thought about dropping it altogether.
Don't drop it. It's the only way you'll be able to map where people come from. Just make it optional so nobody feels pressured.
And the question on why people chose their transport?
That one's really asking two different things: why they use their current method, and what would make them switch to something else. People only answer half of it. Make those two separate questions.
Then there's satisfaction with the bus service. At the moment, it's just an open box. Should we put in an example answer so people know what to write?
An example might lead them. I'd turn it into a rating scale from one to five so you can compare the answers easily.
And the last one's "distance from home to campus". We wondered about moving that to the start, since it's quick to answer.
Actually, you don't need it at all. If you've got the postcode you can work out the distance yourselves, and people usually guess wrong anyway, so I'd take it out.
So we lose one and gain one. That keeps us at fourteen then.
Exactly. Send me the revised version by Friday, and we'll meet again next week.
